short: Singapore has no AI statute. AI governance runs through voluntary IMDA frameworks, led by the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, and the binding layer is the PDPA, with fines of up to S$1 million or 10% of Singapore turnover.
title: Singapore AI Laws
subtitle: No AI act: voluntary IMDA frameworks over a binding privacy law
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI act; the privacy law binds. Singapore governs AI through voluntary frameworks from the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). The newest, the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, was launched on 22 January 2026 and reached version 1.5 on 20 May 2026 (updated 5 June 2026). It binds nobody. What binds is the Personal Data Protection Act 2012, enforced by the Personal Data Protection Commission. Verified on 25 October 2026 against IMDA, the Ministry of Digital Development and Information and the PDPC.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumber or versionPublishedLegal force
Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AIVersion 1.5Launched 22 January 2026; v1.5 published 20 May 2026, updated 5 June 2026Voluntary guidance
Personal Data Protection Act 2012Financial penalties, s. 48JHigher penalty cap from 1 October 2022Binding

Who regulates and enforces

  • IMDA: issues the AI governance frameworks.
  • Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI): the ministry that announced the agentic framework.
  • Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC): enforces the PDPA.

Scope and reach

There is no AI-specific scope. The PDPA applies to organisations that collect, use or disclose personal data; its territorial reach was not re-read on the statute site, which answered this crawler 403, so it is not stated here.

Core obligations

  • No binding AI obligations. The agentic framework organises guidance under four dimensions: bounding the risks, human accountability, technical controls and end-user responsibility.
  • The PDPA's data protection provisions bind any organisation whose AI processes personal data.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Intentional or negligent breach of the PDPA's data protection provisionsUp to S$1 million or 10% of the organisation's annual turnover in Singapore, whichever is higher; the 10% applies where Singapore turnover exceeds S$10 millionPDPA s. 48J, as quoted in the PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Enforcement, para. 27.1PDPC
Any breach of the agentic AI frameworkNone: it is voluntary

What is coming next

No AI bill has been announced. The frameworks are revised as IMDA publishes new versions; the IMDA AI page and the MDDI newsroom are watched weekly.

The wider rulebook

The agentic framework is the newest layer of a stack IMDA has built since 2019. The first Model AI Governance Framework appeared that year and was revised in January 2020. The Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI followed in May 2024 from IMDA and the AI Verify Foundation, and AI Verify itself, a testing framework with software tools, dates from 2022 and has been open source since 2023. In January 2026 IMDA added a Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability. None of these binds; together they are what a Singapore regulator expects a deployer to have read.

Two binding instruments sit beside the PDPA and are easy to miss. On 1 March 2024 the PDPC published its Advisory Guidelines on use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems, which set out how the PDPA's consent, notification and business-improvement provisions apply when personal data trains or feeds an AI system; the guidelines are not law, but the PDPC enforces the PDPA consistently with them. On 15 October 2024 Parliament passed the Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act, introduced by MDDI on 9 September 2024, which amends the Parliamentary Elections Act 1954 and the Presidential Elections Act 1991 to prohibit publishing, boosting or sharing realistic but false depictions of a candidate during an election period, whether made with AI or not, and lets the Returning Officer issue corrective directions. Scam and deepfake misuse outside elections falls under the Online Criminal Harms Act 2023, the Computer Misuse Act 1993 and the Cybersecurity Act 2018.

In practice a company deploying AI in Singapore is audited against three questions: does its data handling meet the PDPA as the 2024 guidelines read it, does its system testing match AI Verify and the LLM starter kit, and, for agents, does it keep a human accountable under the four dimensions of the agentic framework. The IMDA update of May 2026 added case studies drawn from industry feedback, so the framework is now the practical reference, not just the principle.

Last verified

4 November 2026, against the sources above. Not confirmed on an official source and therefore left out: the commencement date of the elections amendment Act, reported as January 2025; the PDPA's territorial reach and the statute's own wording, because Singapore Statutes Online answered this crawler 403; the penalty amounts are as the PDPC's guidelines quote them.
